There are several suggested clinical characteristics of STN, such as onset before the 50s, bilaterality, involvement of the V1 branch, and signs and symptoms of sensory dysfunction. The clinical features differ from those of classical TN, in which the pain is continuous and dull, and the painful episodes last from 3–4 hours [ , ] . According to ICHD-3, the STN is classified as follows: TN due to MS MS is an autoimmune disease that causes axonal degeneration and demyelination in the CNS. The main comorbidities associated with MS are cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, depression, anxiety, and some autoimmune diseases, such as thyroid diseases, IBD, and DM. The incidence of TN increases approximately 20-fold in patients with MS. A total of 1.9%–4.9% of patients with MS suffer from neuropathic pain. On the other hand, MS is found in 2%–14% of patients with TN. Compared with patients without MS, patients with MS have a more severe form of pain, who had to use health care services to manage their pain, and 46.2% reported no remission, whereas 11.5% reported only weeks of remission. In TN secondary to MS, there are no remission periods that are observed in classical and idiopathic TN. Pathognomonic MS lesions are demyelinated areas in the cortex and white matter of the CNS associated with gliosis, axonal loss, inflammation, and incomplete remyelination. As in classical and idiopathic TN, TN secondary to MS affects the right side more than the left and is more common in women than in men. Patients with MS may also have NVC. On the other hand, demyelination of the primary trigeminal afferent intrapontine trigeminal nucleus alone is enough to cause TN [ – ] . Although NVC is characteristic of classical TN, as we mentioned earlier, there is a strong association between NVC and the development of TN in MS. Therefore, it is important to briefly discuss the pathophysiology and molecular alterations that occur in the compressed nerve, which draws parallels classical TN, except for the pattern of demyelination in classical TN, which differs from that seen in MS, since it is mechanically not associated with inflammation [ , ] . As a result of mechanical vascular compression by nearby vessels, several focal alterations occur, including focal demyelination at the entry zone of the trigeminal nerve, atrophy, hypertrophy, and damage to Schwann cells. This alternation leads to an ectopically firing impulse that is generated from this focus [ ] : One of the most accepted hypotheses is the “ignition hypothesis” proposed by Devor et al , which states that “partially damaged neurons trigger a stimulus-induced burst of activity, making them hyperexcitable and susceptible to cross excitation as a result of the physical proximity of the neurons to the root compression site.” Therefore, this makes the neuron more susceptible to minor stimuli and generates abnormal electrical activity, which is then augmented by spread to the nearby neuron (ephaptic interaction) because there is no myelin sheath between them, thereby resulting in sudden onset shock-like pain in the clinic [ ] . Several preclinical and clinical studies support the role of voltage-gated sodium channels (VGSCs) and voltage-gated potassium channels (VGPCs) in the hyperexcitability of the compressed nerve and the generation of ectopic impulses. With respect to VGSCs, preclinical studies using an animal model of TN demonstrated upregulation of Nav1.3 and downregulation of Nav1.7. These findings have also been confirmed by clinical studies, which have shown that patients with TN have the same alterations in VGSCs. Nav1.3 and Nav1.7 are known to contribute to increased neuronal excitability. Therefore, the increase in Nav1.3 could be the pathological form of this condition, whereas a decrease in Nav1.7 could be a compensatory mechanism [ ] . Upregulation of the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv7.2 was noted in the preclinical model, which could also be explained as a compensatory mechanism to reduce excitation. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has demonstrated alterations in the brain structure, functions, and connections between different areas of the brain and the long-term presence of TN. These alterations include changes in gray matter volume, brain activation, and pain processing; all these changes can be linked to disease duration and prognosis. TN due to structural lesions All the diseases in the pathway of the fifth cranial nerve may be responsible for STN. These lesions can be classified as lesions of the nuclei, e.g., ischemia, hemorrhage, tumor, MS plaque, or syringomyelic cavitation; lesions of the root within the cisterns; and Meckel’s cave, e.g., infectious meningitis, carcinomatous meningitis, lymphoma, or neurosarcoidosis; lesions of the cavernous sinus, e.g., meningioma, Schwannoma, or an aneurysm; and distal branch lesions, e.g., schwannoma, sarcoidosis, or ENT cancer [ ] . Figure illustrates the histopathological features of tumors associated with TN. Clinically diagnosed TN with typical symptoms and a good response to medical and pharmacological therapy (such as carbamazepine; see later in “Pharmacological Treatments”) does not exclude, as a cause, the possibility of a tumor compressing the trigeminal nerve. Therefore, it is crucial to investigate patients with TN clinically and with neuroimaging before providing medical treatment. Almost all patients can be free of symptoms of TN after surgical removal of a structural lesion that compresses the nerve (usually in the posterior cranial fossa) [ ] . The pathogenesis of this condition is the same as the pathogenesis of NVC. Thus, compression of the nerve by a nearby tumor will lead to a focal lesion of demyelination, which will make it hyperexcitable and susceptible to firing and generating electrical impulses. Notably, infiltrating malignant tumors can also cause axonal degeneration, resulting in hypoesthesia in regions of the face and persistent pain [ ] . The trigeminal nerve can be compressed at any site during its course, which can lead to TN. Therefore, the most common type of tumor that leads to this phenomenon can be divided according to the anatomical course of the trigeminal nerve starting from the brainstem to the peripheral segment: Traumatic causes Few studies related to this type of TN exist. However, traumatic events such as RTC and iatrogenic procedures such as dental operations and postneurovascular decompression nerve injury can lead to the relapse of TN, which may be taken into account depending on the patient’s history and clinical findings. The pathophysiology of this cause could be related to direct nerve injury from the trauma itself or to the inflammatory process that is related to the trauma that affects the trigeminal nerve [ , ] . TN due to other diseases Inflammatory causes One of the most common causes of STN is MS. Compared with non-MS individuals, MS patients have a 20-fold increased risk of developing TN. The prevalence rate of TN in MS ranges from 2% to 6% in some resources. There is not much difference in the characteristic symptoms between classic TN and MS, so it more often affects women on the right side of the face, but what is unique regarding MS is bilateral involvement of the face in 18% of MS patients (because demyelination plaque may be involved in the midline of the pons where the bilateral nuclei of CN V are located) [ ] . Previous studies emphasized that the pathogenesis of MS-related TN is related mainly to demyelination plaque damaging the trigeminal nerve root entry zone (REZ) in the pons. This demyelination leads to disturbances in normal nerve function, conduction, and excitation, and in some patients, NVC may play a role. However, recent MRI-based research has revealed a significant association between NVC and MS-related TN. This finding suggests a dual mechanism in many patients with TN: inflammatory demyelination caused primarily by MS-related plaques and NVC by nearby blood vessels. This combined effect exacerbates symptoms through a “double-crush” mechanism [ , ] . Most of the studies suggest an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, and one of the most presumed mechanisms is vascular compression, whereas other studies suggest other vascular disorders, calcium ion channel, or VGNC mutations, especially Nav1.6, or inherited anatomical abnormalities and familial hereditary neuropathic disease (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth) [ ] . Another less frequent cause of TN could be systemic diseases such as rheumatologic diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus and scleroderma), and viral infection (usually herpesvirus) may also play a role in this condition [ ] . Notably, a small percentage of TNs (0.22%–1.8%) are caused by arteriovenous malformations, which are usually presented with typical features of classical TNs and cannot distinguish between them. They are usually discovered when the pain becomes refractory to medical therapy or has other signs of neurological deficit that require more investigation with trigeminal reflex assessment (sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 93% for distinguishing between symptomatic and classical TN) and neuroimaging [ ] . Emerging theories While the genetic background of TN is complex, it has a significant role in understanding the pathogenesis of STN, which is supported by several preclinical studies in animal models, so more focus should be given to clinical studies to illuminate the genetic factors involved in the pathogenesis of TN [ ] . There is a lack of studies regarding the pathogenesis of some causes of STN, such as trauma-related TN, and how it differs in pathogenesis and at the molecular level from posttraumatic trigeminal neuropathic pain. Focusing on these topics will help in understanding the clinical symptoms of TN and choosing the best treatment strategy [ ] . Clinical presentation TN has been described previously as one of the most incapacitating orofacial pains. In 1773, John Fothergill suggested a clinical description of TN; however, until 1820, Dr Charles Bell identified the symptoms of facial pain and recognized the clinical picture of the disease. TN is characterized by unilateral, sudden, brief, severe, and stabbing episodes of pain in one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve. Pain is described as sharp, electric-like, or shock-like, superficial episodes associated with tic-like cramps of the facial muscles, which explains why it is called “tic douloureux.” Approximately 60% of cases are unilateral, involving the mandibular or maxillary branches, and 35% of cases involve both. However, less than 4% of cases involve the ophthalmic branch. Bilateral concomitant pain is rare (1.7%–5%), and these patients usually experience side-alternating pain [ ] . Aging is considered a risk factor for the development of TN, most commonly in patients over 50 years of age, and it has a sex predilection in which the incidence in women is greater than that in men at a ratio of 2–3:1. In 60% of patients, the right side of the face was affected more than the left side [ ] . One of the hallmarks of clinical presentations of TN is triggerability by mild mechanical stimulation, in which pain attacks usually occur in response to stimulating triggers in areas innervated by trigeminal nerve branches. Examples of such triggering events include talking, chewing, drinking, tooth brushing, fine touching of the face, shaving, washing or drying, smiling, and putting on makeup. The trigger areas most commonly involved are the upper lip, lateral part of the lower lip, nasolabial fold, alveolar gingiva, cheek, and chin. TN patients may experience a reduction in quality of life due to the severity of pain, and some patients might be exposed to anxiety and depression [ ] . Diagnostic approach TN is principally a clinical diagnosis on the basis of a comprehensive history and neurological examination, which makes laboratory tests and imaging techniques not mandatory for making a diagnosis. However, patients with TN should undergo MRI to assess any NVC. The gold standard imaging test for STN is MRI, but when it is contraindicated, CT of the head is appropriate. In 15% of patients, STN occurs due to a tumor in the cerebellopontine angle or MS. Linear plaques in the ventrolateral pons can be detected via T2-weighted MRI between trigeminal nuclei and the trigeminal REZ in patients with TN secondary to MS. MRI has 100% specificity, 98% sensitivity, 93% positive predictive value, and 97% negative predictive value [ – ] . Does not fit with another ICHD-3 diagnosis. Management Medical therapy should be the first-line approach for managing TN. Abortive therapy is typically ineffective because of the brief duration of attacks. The cornerstone of management is pharmacological preventive therapy, although acute treatments may be used for severe exacerbations. Surgery is generally considered only after two failed medical treatment attempts, with 33%–50% of patients eventually requiring surgical intervention. Management of STN For patients with STN (e.g., due to tumors), treatment should focus on addressing the underlying pathology, such as tumor resection or decompression, to achieve pain relief. For patients who are not surgical candidates, medical management is offered for symptomatic control. Acute treatment for severe exacerbation Acute TN attacks are characterized by a high frequency of pain, which can lead to dehydration and anorexia due to the inability to eat or drink. Hospital admission may be required for rehydration, correction of nutritional status, and titration of antiepileptic drugs. Opioids, although commonly used, are ineffective and should be avoided [ ] . Topical lidocaine injections into trigger zones can provide transient pain relief. On the basis of clinical experience, intravenous infusions of fosphenytoin (15 mg/kg over 30 minutes) and lidocaine (5 mg/kg over 60 minutes) are effective for acute attacks and should be administered under cardiac monitoring by trained healthcare professionals [ ] . Pharmacological preventive long-term treatment The long-term management of TN often involves the use of antiepileptic and neuropathic pain medications, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin, pregabalin, baclofen, and botulinum toxin. First-line treatments Carbamazepine (200–1200 mg/day) and oxcarbazepine (300–1800 mg/day) are the primary drugs used for long-term treatment. These medications provide initial pain relief in approximately 90% of patients. Carbamazepine is the drug of choice, although it is associated with side effects such as hyponatremia, aplastic anemia, and liver failure, as well as metabolic interactions with other drugs. Compared with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine causes fewer side effects and has fewer drug interactions, although it can cause more central nervous system depression and dose-related hyponatremia. These drugs may be less well tolerated by women, and their efficacy can vary between individuals. Notably, 200 mg of carbamazepine is approximately equivalent to 300 mg of oxcarbazepine. Patients on these medications should be closely monitored with baseline and periodic tests, including sodium levels, complete blood count, and liver function tests. While carbamazepine remains the best-supported standard treatment for TN, oxcarbazepine has been shown to provide significant additional pain relief for patients unresponsive to carbamazepine, with 37.1% of patients reporting improved pain control and 67.5% reducing their pain days by at least 50%. Thus, oxcarbazepine may be considered a salvage therapy for patients for whom carbamazepine monotherapy fails [ , , ] . Second-line treatments (lamotrigine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin-type pregabalin, baclofen, or phenytoin) Either as an add-on or given as monotherapy. The recommendation of Botulinum toxin type A was an important addition to the European Academy of Neurology guidelines. Surgical treatment of STN According to the European Academy of Neurology, medical management, including adequate dosing and regular monitoring, is recommended before surgery for TN can be considered. A prospective study reported that 65% of patients referred to a specialized center could be managed medically for up to 2 years, whereas 35% ultimately required surgical intervention. There is no scientific evidence supporting early surgery in the disease course [ , ] . MVD MVD is the first-choice surgical intervention for patients with classical TN. Although it is the most invasive technique, it offers superior outcomes, with a pain-free rate of 62%–89% after 3 years of follow-up. The annual risk of recurrence is less than 2% after 5 years and less than 1% after 10 years. Complications following MVD occur in up to 20% of patients, although serious complications are rare. MVD is recommended for patients with inadequate pain control, a life expectancy of more than 5 years, and those who can tolerate a small craniotomy. However, it is not routinely recommended for patients with MS, as the failure rate is high. This is likely due to demyelination extending into the brainstem, which complicates treatment in MS patients. Moreover, MS patients often present at a younger age and may experience bilateral facial pain. For MS patients, other treatments, such as percutaneous procedures or radiosurgery, are preferred [ , ] . Percutaneous balloon compression Percutaneous balloon compression of the Gasserian ganglion is a less invasive procedure that primarily damages thick myelinated fibers while leaving thinner myelinated and unmyelinated fibers relatively unharmed. The procedure works by blocking VGSCs, which stabilize hyperexcited neuronal membranes and inhibit repetitive firing. The correct balloon pressure is confirmed when the balloon’s pear-shaped insufflation indicates proper placement, and any abnormal protrusion into the prepontine cistern requires repositioning. Balloon compression has a low complication rate, making it particularly beneficial for elderly patients and allowing for repeat procedures if symptoms persist. In patients with STN, Gasserian ganglion procedures are recommended unless vascular compression is evident on MRI. Percutaneous radiofrequency rhizotomy Radiofrequency rhizotomy has a high initial success rate of approximately 90%, although recurrence occurs in approximately 25% of cases, with a long-term response rate of 57.7% after five years. The principle of percutaneous radiofrequency rhizotomy involves differential coagulation of the A-delta and C fibers (which mediate pain) and A-beta fibers (which mediate touch). The electrode tip is heated to 70 °C for 70 s, and after each thermal lesion, the patient is awakened for sensory stimulation testing. For the first procedure, a mild hypalgesic lesion (less than 50% loss of pain perception with preserved touch sensation) is made. For recurrent pain after previous procedures, a more substantial hypalgesic lesion (greater than 75% loss of pain perception with preserved touch sensation) is created. This procedure’s relative ease allows for additional treatments in patients with recurring pain [ ] . Stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife) Gamma knife radiosurgery (GKR) is a noninvasive frame-based technique that delivers radiation via a fixed cobalt source. The treatment is performed in a single session on the same day as the planning. During the procedure, a stereotactic Leksell frame is placed under local anesthesia, and radiation from stationary Cobalt-60 sources is aimed at the trigeminal REZ from multiple angles. In GKR, the target is typically placed approximately 7.5 mm anterior to the REZ along the cisternal segment of the trigeminal nerve. This target area is selected to maximize radiation delivery to the sensory fibers while minimizing risk to adjacent brainstem structures. However, the exact target may vary slightly depending on individual anatomical variations and institutional protocols. Targeting is typically guided by high-resolution MRI and stereotactic planning

Development of treatment options A novel drug, BIB074 (formerly known as CNV1014802 or lamotrigine), a state-dependent sodium channel blocker, completed a phase II trial with promising results. This drug showed efficacy in reducing the frequency of paroxysms and overall pain severity in both primary and STN patients, although it was not statistically significant at its primary endpoint. Prognosis The prognosis for STN changes depending on the underlying cause, but in general, it is less favorable than that for primary (idiopathic) TN. STN is more difficult to treat than primary TN. It is typically caused by underlying conditions such as MS, a tumor, vascular compression, and additional neurological symptoms and signs depending on the underlying causes, such as somatosensory deficits, auditory disturbances, or other cranial nerve impairments, which can be challenging to manage. Patients with STN may experience more frequent and severe pain that is less responsive to medication, and the pain is also more persistent and difficult to control over time [ ] . The prognosis is often worse for patients with STN caused by MS. If STN is caused by vascular compression or a tumor, the prognosis may be better if the underlying cause can be successfully treated or managed (medications such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentinoids may be used). Compared with primary TN, surgical treatments such as rhizotomy, GKR, or MVD may be less effective for treating STN, which has high rates of recurrence or incomplete pain relief. Surgical intervention, such as MVD, is the most common surgical procedure and is effective for treating patients with STN for long-term treatment; however, the recurrence rate of all patients treated with MVD is high, so a second operation is needed. The factors associated with increased recurrence rates are female sex, symptoms lasting more than 8 years, venous compression of the trigeminal nerve, and a lack of immediate pain relief after initial surgery [ ] . GKR is a noninvasive procedure and is another way to treat STN, especially if the cause is a tumor or vascular compression. This intervention results in less recurrence than MVD does and fewer complications than microsurgery does; however, the response is usually slower than that of other treatments, and GKR targeting the trigeminal nerve has shown reasonable and longer-lasting pain reduction than radiation therapy targeting the tumor alone when GKR is used for tumors related to STN, resulting in good pain relief after GKR and a high recurrence rate. The prognosis depends on the specific type of tumor causing STN. For example, in patients with STN caused by meningiomas or vestibular schwannomas, pain relief is improved by approximately 80% after stereotactic radiosurgery compared with other tumor types. This procedure has a recurrence rate that should be closely monitored, and a multidisciplinary approach to management is important for these patients. One study compared the outcomes of open surgery versus stereotactic radiosurgery for tumor-related STN and reported that both modalities can be effective, with the radiosurgery option being safer and having lower morbidity than open surgery does, and the recurrence rate with radiosurgery is higher than that with open surgery is. Prognostic and diagnostic factors STN poses unique diagnostic challenges because of its diverse etiologies and overlapping clinical features with classical trigeminal neuralgia (CTN). While STN is often associated with underlying structural lesions such as tumors, MS, or vascular malformations, early identification remains critical for timely intervention and better outcomes. Clinically, STN is more likely to present with constant or background facial pain in addition to paroxysmal attacks and is frequently associated with sensory deficits upon examination – features that distinguish it from CTN and may serve as early diagnostic clues [ , ] . Neuroimaging, particularly high-resolution MRI with constructive interference at steady state (CISS) sequences, remains the gold standard for detecting causative lesions such as demyelination or neoplasms [ ] . High-resolution MRI, particularly using sequences such as 3D CISS and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, is essential for detecting causative lesions in the STN. In MS-related STN, hyperintense lesions along the intrapontine segment of the trigeminal root entry zone have been correlated with the presence and severity of neuralgia [ ] . Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) has also shown promise in revealing microstructural damage to the trigeminal nerve, providing a potential imaging biomarker for disease monitoring [ ] . Neurophysiological studies, including trigeminal reflex testing and blink reflex assessments, can help differentiate between primary and secondary forms by revealing abnormalities in central pathways, especially in the MS-related STN [ ] . Recent studies have also suggested the potential role of DTI in evaluating microstructural changes in trigeminal pathways, suggesting that DTI is a promising noninvasive diagnostic tool [ ] . Moreover, genetic studies, although limited, have explored mutations linked to familial syndromes (e.g., neurofibromatosis) that may predispose individuals to secondary neuralgias [ ] . Prognostically, delayed diagnosis is associated with worse pain control and greater treatment resistance, underscoring the importance of a comprehensive diagnostic workup [ ] . The incorporation of emerging diagnostic technologies such as machine learning-assisted imaging analysis and serum biomarkers (e.g., neurofilament light chain in MS-related STN) may further enhance early detection and prediction of outcomes [ , ] . Burden of disease STN imposes a substantial burden on both individual patients and healthcare systems because of its chronic, debilitating nature and often complex etiology. Unlike classical TN, the STN is frequently associated with underlying structural or demyelinating lesions, such as tumors or MS, which contribute to diagnostic delays and treatment resistance [ , ] . Patients with STN often experience continuous, burning pain superimposed on lancinating episodes, leading to significantly reduced quality of life, poor sleep, anxiety, depression, and social isolation [ ] . A recent multicenter study revealed that individuals with STN have higher pain interference scores and lower physical functioning than do those with classical TN, reflecting the disproportionate psychosocial impact of the disease [ ] . Moreover, treatment is often prolonged and complex, requiring multimodal pain management, imaging, surgical interventions, and regular follow-up, which contribute to increased direct healthcare costs and indirect costs such as lost productivity and long-term disability [ , ] . In patients with MS-related STN, health care resource utilization – including MRI monitoring, neurology visits, and neuropathic medication use – is significantly greater than that in MS patients without facial pain [ ] . Given these implications, improving early recognition and targeted management of STN is critical for reducing patient suffering and minimizing socioeconomic consequences. Conclusion In conclusion, STN represents a distinct and often underrecognized clinical entity that demands accurate diagnosis and individualized management. Unlike classical TN, STN arises from identifiable structural or pathological causes, necessitating the use of advanced neuroimaging and multidisciplinary evaluation for proper characterization. Management strategies should be tailored to the underlying etiology, integrating pharmacologic therapy, surgical intervention, or neuromodulation when appropriate. While current treatments offer symptom relief, durable outcomes remain challenging owing to the complex and heterogeneous nature of STN. This review highlights the pressing need for high-quality, multicenter prospective studies to establish evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic guidelines. A multidisciplinary, etiology-driven approach remains central to improving patient outcomes and advancing clinical care in this challenging condition. Limitations This review is subject to certain limitations, most notably the nature of the available literature. The evidence base for STN is predominantly composed of case reports and case series, with a lack of large-scale observational studies or randomized trials. This reflects the current state of research in this area, which is likely due to the rarity and heterogeneity of the condition. Consequently, while the findings presented here offer valuable insights, they should be interpreted with caution, and further high-quality clinical studies are needed to validate these observations.
